Mellophone 起源於19世紀號角設計熱潮，早期Koenig horn採用: The mellophone came out of the nineteenth-century boom in horn design; the early Koenig horn used piston valves and its shape was influenced by the post horn. The name mellophone was later used for horns similar to the Distin, and the traditional circular model, mostly in F, replaced the French horn in school and community bands. After the middle of the twentieth century the traditional model declined; American drum and bugle corps used mellophones in G until around 2000, when the rules on key were relaxed and that changed. In 1957 the bell-front Mellophonium appeared, and Stan Kenton used a section of four from the 1960s.

行進圓號的音色主要受吹嘴影響：使用深杯、內徑較寬的吹嘴時，聲音較暗而圓；改用類似: The mellophone's timbre depends mainly on the mouthpiece: with a deep cup and a wide bore the sound is darker and rounder; with a trumpet-like cup mouthpiece it is brighter and closer to a trumpet; when a French horn player uses a funnel mouthpiece with an adapter the timbre is softer and warmer, close to the French horn. Its bell faces forward and the tubing is shorter, which helps project the sound forward outdoors on the march; the smaller bore also makes a larger volume easier than on a marching French horn. The overtone series of an F mellophone is an octave above that of an F French horn, and the fingering is close to the trumpet.
行進圓號（Mellophone）是氣鳴銅管樂器，H-S編號423.232，通常為: The mellophone is an aerophone of the brass family, H-S 423.232, usually in F, with a conical bore and piston valves, played with the right hand and fingered like a trumpet. Its bell faces forward, which makes it easy to project the sound outdoors on the march, so it is common in marching bands and drum and bugle corps in place of the French horn. Its tubing is shorter than the French horn's and its overtone series higher; in playing, the tuning slide or the first-valve slide is adjusted.
